findings.title: Missing prisma import — file will not compile
findings.body: The newly added refresh block calls `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, ... })` at line 96, but the file's import list (lines 1–21) never imports `prisma` from `@calcom/prisma`. This is a TypeScript compile error (`Cannot find name 'prisma'`), so the package/build fails whenever this file is type-checked.

findings.title: Refreshed Salesforce tokens are saved but the stale access token is used
findings.body: In `getClient`, the code fetches a fresh token set from Salesforce, validates it, and writes it to the DB (lines 75–99), but then constructs the `jsforce.Connection` with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` and `instanceUrl: credentialKey.instance_url` — the old, possibly-expired credential values — instead of `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`. The refresh is therefore useless for the current session: the connection is built on the stale token the refresh was meant to replace. Additionally, this refresh now runs unconditionally on every service instantiation (extra token request + DB write per operation, even when the token is still valid), and it never goes through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so when credential syncing is enabled and the stored key has no valid Salesforce refresh token, every Salesforce calendar operation throws.

findings.title: credentialId passed as userId to refreshOAuthTokens
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(refreshFunction, appSlug, userId)` expects the Cal.com user id as its third argument, which it sends to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. In zoho-bigin's `refreshAccessToken`, the third argument is `credentialId` (the credential row's primary key), not `credential.userId`. With credential sync enabled, the self-hoster's endpoint receives a credential id as the user id, so it will look up and return tokens for the wrong (or no) user, and the resulting tokens get written onto this user's credential.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema's computed keys don't work — expiry fields are silently stripped
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()` do not create zod catchalls: `z.string().toString()` evaluates to a constant string ("[object Object]"), so the schema is effectively just `{ access_token: z.string() }` plus a meaningless literal key. Because zod object schemas strip unknown keys by default, parsing a sync-endpoint response like `{ access_token, expires_in }` or the mutated Google credentials object drops every property except `access_token` — including the expiry. Consequence: in sync mode the credentials written to the DB (e.g. Google at `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:97`) lose `expiry_date`, so the token is considered expired on every subsequent call and the expiry returned by the sync endpoint is never persisted. Zod's `.catchall()`/`.passthrough()` was presumably intended.

findings.title: Literal "refresh_token" placeholder overwrites real refresh tokens in the DB
findings.body: When the parsed token response has no `refresh_token`, the code invents one: `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. This runs in both modes, not just sync mode. In `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:264` the parsed data is merged over the stored credentials (`{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`) and persisted, so if Microsoft's token endpoint omits `refresh_token` in a refresh response (which the schema explicitly allows via `.optional()`), the user's real refresh token in the database is replaced by the string "refresh_token". The next refresh then fails with invalid_grant and the user's calendar disconnects — a regression for existing Office 365 users even with credential syncing disabled.

findings.title: Sync branch returns a raw fetch Response while callers expect provider-shaped objects
findings.body: When credential sync is enabled this helper returns the unparsed `fetch` `Response` from `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, but the fallback branch returns whatever each provider's refresh function returns (googleapis `res` with `.data`, an axios response with `.data`, a Hubspot token object). Callers were not adapted to the Response shape: `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:94` does `res?.data` (undefined on a Response, so `token.access_token` throws a TypeError that is swallowed by the catch and the refresh silently no-ops, leaving the expired token in use); `hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:177` treats the Response as a `HubspotToken`, producing `expiryDate = NaN` and `setAccessToken(undefined)`; `zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts:217` and `zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts:96` read `.data` on a Response (TypeError, caught and logged, so the token is never refreshed). As written, enabling sync breaks token refresh for these apps.

findings.title: Webex still enforces provider-specific token schema, rejecting sync-endpoint responses
findings.body: Unlike zoom/google/office365calendar, the webex refresh path was not switched to `parseRefreshTokenResponse` — it still parses the response with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema`, which requires `scope` and `token_type` string literals, `refresh_token`, and `refresh_token_expires_in`. Per the PR's own contract the sync endpoint returns only an access token and an expiry, so in sync mode parsing always fails and `refreshAccessToken` rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned", making Webex meetings unusable whenever credential syncing is enabled.

findings.title: Sync response expiry is discarded, and stored key loses refresh_token
findings.body: After the refresh call, the code computes `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000)` and then overwrites the entire stored credential key with `responseBody`. The sync endpoint contract is "access token and expiry date", not necessarily `expires_in`; if it returns anything else (e.g. `expiry_date`), that value is clobbered with ~now, so `isExpired` is always true and every `getToken()` call hits the sync endpoint again. The wholesale key replacement also drops `refresh_token` from the stored credential, so if syncing is later disabled the credential can no longer refresh.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time !==
findings.body: The shared webhook secret is verified with a plain string `!==` comparison between the header value and `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. For a long-lived bearer secret protecting an endpoint that writes arbitrary credential keys for any user, this should use a constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual`) to avoid leaking the secret byte-by-byte through response timing.

findings.title: Malformed input causes unhandled 500s; no HTTP method check
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` (line 31), `symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, ...)` and the surrounding `JSON.parse` (lines 57–59) all throw on invalid input (bad body shape, wrong encryption key, non-JSON plaintext), producing an unhandled 500 with a stack trace instead of a 4xx response. The handler also accepts any HTTP method, so a GET (empty body) takes the same crash path. Wrap validation/decryption in try/catch and reject non-POST methods.

findings.title: No tests for the credential-sync webhook or refresh-sync paths
findings.body: The PR adds a security-sensitive endpoint that decrypts and overwrites user credentials, plus a new token-refresh code path in nine app integrations, and the author explicitly states no tests were added. Given the multiple mode-dependent behaviors (sync on/off, per-app response shapes), at minimum the webhook's auth/upsert logic and `refreshOAuthTokens`/`parseRefreshTokenResponse` need unit tests before merge.
